🕊️ Reish Lakish's Challenge — why isn't the same leniency taught for unspecified bird-offering money?

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Money, Blood, and Wine — When Does Sanctity End?
overview.subtitle: Meilah 11a–11b
overview.hebrewSource: הַדָּם – קַל בַּתְּחִלָּה וְחָמוּר בְּסוֹפוֹ. נְסָכִין – חוֹמֶר בִּתְחִלָּתָן וְקַל בְּסוֹפָן
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: After closing the mishna on sin offerings left to die, the daf turns to a nazirite who set aside undesignated money for his three completion offerings — no me'ilah applies, since any of it could become the peace offering, which is only subject to me'ilah after its blood is sprinkled. Reish Lakish's attempt to extend this leniency to bird-offering money is rejected by Rava. A new mishna then presents Rabbi Shimon's elegant symmetry: blood begins lenient and ends strict, while libation wine begins strict and ends lenient. The Gemara traces this to a dispute about whether blood is Temple property at all, and explores the principle of 'two verses that come as one' — a hint that some rules (like ashes remaining subject to misuse even after their mitzva is done) are narrow exceptions, not models for other cases.

callout.label: Reish Lakish's challenge:
callout.text: Why not teach the same leniency for undesignated bird-offering money (for a leper or new mother)? Rava answers: the Torah directs undesignated nazirite money toward a valid peace offering, but undesignated bird money would need to buy birds unfit for the altar (too young or too old) — not a comparable case.

slides.title: 🩸 Rabbi Shimon's Mishna: A Mirror-Image Pattern
slides.subtitle: Blood and libation wine trade places on the leniency/stringency scale

lines.speaker: R' Shimon
lines.text: Blood is lenient at the start, strict at the end: before sprinkling, no me'ilah applies; but once its remainder flows out through the canal to the Kidron Valley — now you ARE liable for me'ilah.

lines.speaker: R' Shimon
lines.text: Libation wine is the reverse — strict at the start, lenient at the end: from the moment it's consecrated, me'ilah applies; but once it descends into the altar's drainpipes (shitin), its mitzva is done and me'ilah no longer applies.

lines.speaker: Rabbis (baraita)
lines.text: We disagree about the blood at the end: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon say me'ilah applies once it reaches the Kidron; we say it does NOT — blood was never Temple property to begin with.

lines.speaker: Ulla / Beit R' Yishmael
lines.text: The verse 'I have given it to you upon the altar' (Lev. 17:11) means the blood belongs to YOU (the people), given for atonement, not for misuse liability — so it's never subject to me'ilah at all.

callout.label: R' Yoḥanan's proof:
callout.text: 'For it is the blood that atones' (Lev. 17:11) — its status before atonement equals its status after: since there's no me'ilah after atonement (the mitzva is done), there was none before either.

slides.title: 📜 Why Doesn't 'Trumat HaDeshen' Prove Sanctity Can Outlast Its Mitzva?
slides.subtitle: Testing R' Yoḥanan's symmetry argument against a known exception

nodes.content: ❓ Challenge: couldn't the SAME logic run backward — before atonement equals AFTER, so blood should carry me'ilah even after atonement?
🔄 Rejected: is there any precedent for an item whose mitzva is done yet still carries me'ilah? — Yes! Trumat hadeshen (ash removal), even once performed, remains subject to me'ilah

🚫 Answer: trumat hadeshen is paired with the scapegoat's limbs (or the High Priest's Yom Kippur garments, or the broken-necked heifer) as 'two verses that come as one' — a rule shared by only two special cases NEVER generalizes further
✅ So trumat hadeshen cannot serve as a precedent for blood — the symmetry argument for 'no me'ilah, before or after atonement' survives intact

callout.label: Multiple pairings tested:
callout.text: The Gemara runs through several possible partner-verses for trumat hadeshen (the scapegoat, priestly garments, the broken-necked heifer), each blocked by its own textual exclusion, showing the exception truly stays contained.

slides.title: 🍇 The Once-in-Seventy-Years Ritual
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok's account of congealed libation wine
slides.hebrewSource: כְּשֵׁם שֶׁנִּיסּוּכָהּ בִּקְדוּשָּׁה, כָּךְ שְׂרֵיפָתָהּ בִּקְדוּשָּׁה
slides.label: The account:
slides.text: A small gap between the ramp and the altar led down to the drainpipes. Once every seventy years, young priests descended to remove congealed wine — resembling pressed fig-cakes — accumulated from decades of libations, and burned it in sanctity within the courtyard, derived by verbal analogy ('holy'/'holy') from the law of burning leftover offerings. This seems to contradict the mishna's claim that libation wine loses its sanctity once it reaches the drainpipes — resolved by distinguishing wine that merely collected on the way down (still subject to misuse, needing sanctified burning) from wine that actually reached the very bottom of the pipes (which the mishna says is no longer subject to misuse); alternatively, the requirement to burn it in sanctity may be only a rabbinic stringency, supported but not required by the verse.

slides.title: 🕯️ Final New Mishna: More Items With No Real Me'ilah
slides.subtitle: Ash removal, menorah wicks, and unfit birds
rows: Ash removed from the inner altar, or menorah wicks
Forbidden to benefit from ab initio, but no me'ilah if one does
Doves too young / pigeons too old for sacrifice
Forbidden to benefit from ab initio, but no me'ilah if one does — since they were never fit for the altar in the first place

summary.principle: Me'ilah tracks genuine consecrated status, not merely formal handling: undesignated money that could still become a valid offering avoids me'ilah, blood may never have been Temple property at all, and narrow textual exceptions like trumat hadeshen — bound by the rule that 'two verses that come as one' don't generalize — cannot be used to prove that sanctity can outlast a completed mitzva elsewhere.

🩸 R' Shimon's mishna: blood — lenient then strict; libations — strict then lenient

columns.content: 📜 Blood may never be Temple property — 'I have given it to YOU' (Lev. 17:11)
🍇 Congealed libation wine, once every 70 years, burned 'in sanctity' — reconciled with the mishna's rule

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: exceptions like trumat hadeshen are textually locked to their partner cases and cannot generalize to prove sanctity ever outlasts a completed mitzva

quiz.q: Why is there no liability for me'ilah when one derives benefit from a nazirite's undesignated offering money?
o: Because nazirite offerings are never consecrated
Because all the money is fit to purchase the peace offering, which is subject to me'ilah only after its blood is sprinkled
Because nazirites are exempt from all Temple obligations
Because the money technically belongs to the priests
quiz.e: The mishna explains that since the undesignated money could always be used for the peace offering — subject to me'ilah only after sprinkling — there's no definite me'ilah liability before that point.

quiz.q: How does Rava respond to Reish Lakish's challenge that the mishna should also exempt undesignated money for bird offerings (nests)?
o: He agrees and says the mishna is incomplete
He distinguishes the cases: the Torah explicitly directs nazirite money toward a valid peace offering, but bird money would only buy birds unfit for the altar (too young or too old)
He says bird offerings are never subject to me'ilah regardless
He says nazirites never bring bird offerings
quiz.e: Rava explains that unlike the nazirite's money, which can always fund a fit peace offering, money set aside for unspecified bird nests could only purchase birds that are unfit for sacrifice — not a comparable exemption.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Shimon's mishna, how do blood and libation wine differ in their me'ilah timeline?
o: Both follow identical rules

Blood starts lenient (no me'ilah) and becomes strict (me'ilah applies) after flowing to the Kidron Valley; libation wine starts strict (me'ilah applies) and becomes lenient (no me'ilah) once it reaches the drainpipes
Blood is never subject to me'ilah at any point
Libation wine is always subject to me'ilah
quiz.e: Rabbi Shimon describes a mirror-image pattern: blood moves from no-me'ilah to me'ilah, while libation wine moves from me'ilah to no-me'ilah, as their sanctity 'expires' at different points.

quiz.q: What principle does the Gemara use to explain why the removal of the ashes (trumat hadeshen) — subject to me'ilah even after its mitzva is completed — cannot prove that blood should likewise remain subject to me'ilah after atonement?
o: The principle that ashes are never truly consecrated
The principle that 'two verses that come as one' (two textually linked exceptional cases) do not generalize to teach other cases
The principle that only blood-related halakhot can be compared to each other
There is no such principle; the Gemara simply asserts it as fact
quiz.e: The Gemara identifies trumat hadeshen as paired with another exceptional case (like the scapegoat's limbs) under the rule that two verses sharing a halakha in common do not extend that halakha elsewhere.

quiz.q: What does Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok describe happening once every seventy years at the altar?
o: The altar was completely rebuilt
Young priests removed congealed libation wine from the drainpipes and burned it in sanctity
The Temple was reconsecrated
All unused sacrificial blood was collected and buried
quiz.e: He describes how congealed wine, resembling pressed fig-cakes, accumulated in the altar's drainpipes over decades and was periodically removed and burned in sanctity by young priests.
